title: **I’ve been building a 3D world/platform with AI\-assisted development — here’s the result**
author: lukodiablo
selftext:
I wanted to share a progress update from a project I’ve been working on called Sector Blaster.

It runs on Godot and is designed as a lightweight, browser-based 3D platform inside Discord, rather than a traditional game that people need to download and install.

The video shows the current Plaza, followed by a survival environment called Wolf Valley. The player explores the world and eventually gets defeated by a bear.

What interests me most is the process behind it. I’ve been using AI-assisted development to help build and iterate on a project that includes 3D environments, gameplay systems, multiplayer functionality, and a world-building system. Some of the 3D assets are AI-generated too — for example, the portals in the Plaza was generated with Meshy AI, although it still needs some manual adjustments before it’s ready for use in the game.

AI makes some parts of development faster, but it doesn’t remove the need to test things in the actual engine, deal with performance constraints, or fix problems when different systems interact.

This is a look at the project as it exists today, not a claim that everything is finished. I’m continuing to work on it.

For other developers using AI to build larger projects: what has been your experience moving from individual AI-generated features to getting an entire system working together?

I’d be interested in hearing what others have learned from building something beyond a small prototype.

comments.author: thyros_2028
comments.body: Looks good. When integrating multiple features, I treat it as a software integration, just the basic unit testing and integration testing has worked for me. Maybe treating it like putting multiple components together to build a software helps.

replies.author: lukodiablo
replies.body:
Thanks, that's a good point. I've actually put quite a bit of thought into the architecture around this. Sector has multiple integrations, but the goal is to keep them modular so individual providers can be swapped out or decommissioned without breaking unrelated systems.

Cloudflare also handles a lot of the backend heavy lifting, so I'm not trying to build every infrastructure component myself. The bigger challenge is making sure the boundaries between systems hold up as the platform grows, and testing that everything behaves correctly in the actual game.

There's a lot more integration under the hood than the video shows
